A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cond-FiP research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated between appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-SCM and C-Suite experiments, a Sachs-data evaluation, decoder ablations and larger-context tests.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds inferred-graph, scarce-data, encoder-ablation, distribution-shift and CausalNF experiments.

M1.justification: The encoder, conditional decoder, conditioning operations, MSE objectives and fixed-point generation procedure are retained. V2 expands their explanation and evaluates the inferred-graph input option already described in v1 Section 3.1.

E1.justification: V2 broadens evaluation to unavailable true graphs using AVICI estimates (Appendix C), and progressively shifted mechanism and noise distributions (Appendix E.3). These change input conditions and evaluated distributions. The existing synthetic families, C-Suite and Sachs coverage remain.

E2.justification: CausalNF becomes an evaluated comparator for noise prediction and sample generation in Appendix F, Tables 25–26. FiP, DECI and DoWhy remain in the retained comparisons; DoWhy is excluded from the new 50-sample tests because of reported training problems.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50- and 100-sample contexts, shared AVICI-estimated graphs for all compared methods, encoder training restricted to LIN or RFF, and shift factors of 1, 2, 5 and 10. The original training configuration, 400/400 evaluation split and RMSE definition are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds encoder-training ablations, robustness tests using estimated graphs, scarce-context studies and controlled sensitivity analyses separating mechanism shifts from noise shifts. The original decoder ablation and 1000-sample analysis remain in Appendices E.2 and G.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean RMSE and standard errors across sampled test SCMs. The added experiments largely continue this practice; no new seed information, repeated-training counts, confidence-interval procedure or significance testing is introduced.

E6.justification: All nine original tables retain their numerical values after matching renumbering. V2 adds results for the new evaluations and analyses. For example, Table 11 reports 20-node RFF IN noise RMSE of 0.16 for Cond-FiP versus 0.33 for FiP with 50 samples. Table 22 shows 100-node RFF OUT noise RMSE increasing from 0.16 to 0.44 as the noise-shift factor increases from 1 to 10.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds an explicit generative-map construction and inverse-map derivation, including invertibility under the ANM assumption and its connection to noise recovery. The original SCM assumptions, attention equations and training objectives remain.

C1.justification: The central zero-shot SCM-learning, generation and competitive-performance claims remain. V2's contribution list adds superiority in scarce-data regimes and explicitly identifies additive-noise SCMs, an assumption already stated in v1's background.

C2.justification: V2 attributes scarce-data advantages to learned inductive bias and qualifies distributional robustness by distinguishing mechanism-shift robustness from noise-shift sensitivity, particularly for RFF models. It also discusses the encoder's ANM dependence. The larger-context limitation highlighted in the conclusion was already present in v1 Appendix C.

D1.justification: V2 adds a GitHub code-access link in the abstract and explicit LIN/RFF parameter-support details in Appendix E.3. Previously reported architecture sizes, optimization settings, training budget and L40 hardware remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Gordon et al., Müller et al., Akyürek et al. and Nilforoshan et al., and expands discussion of amortization, in-context learning and treatment-effect estimation. Its central positioning around learning functional mechanisms rather than only causal structures remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and amortized-related-work discussion receive substantial rewriting. Related work becomes a separate section, the setup and inference explanations expand, and the appendices are reorganized into an indexed A–G structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 3's context-size comparison and 20 tables displaying the new experiments and analyses, including tables organized by shift severity. Existing displays are retained, with Figure 1 resized, Figure 2 relocated and appendix tables renumbered.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central generalization argument: Appendix C tests the previously suggested inferred-graph pipeline, Appendix D establishes behavior with scarce contexts, and Appendix E.3 identifies a specific noise-shift failure boundary. These address important empirical gaps while preserving the original results. Added code-access information and methodological explanations further improve the paper's usefulness and reproducibility.
